This is worth isolating, because it is a genuine source of confusion. Aggregation bias, as this chapter defines
it, is a Jensen gap between "predict at the mean" and "average the predictions." Non-collapsibility is the
statement that the odds ratio, specifically, changes when you marginalize a conditional model over a covariate,
even a covariate that is not a confounder. On the logit scale these are two names for one piece of arithmetic:
marginalizing the conditional logistic model over the case mix *is* the integral @eq-agg-aggregate-mean, and the
gap it opens between the conditional-at-the-mean contrast and the marginal contrast *is* the non-collapsibility
of the odds ratio. The worked example shows the marginal odds ratio $e^{1.22}=3.39$ pulled toward the null
relative to the conditional $e^{1.30}=3.67$; this attenuation toward the null is the characteristic direction of
odds-ratio non-collapsibility for a covariate that affects the outcome, and it is why a marginal odds ratio from
an aggregate trial and a conditional odds ratio from a patient-level model are not directly comparable numbers.

Two practical consequences follow. First, an analyst must decide which estimand the decision maker wants; ML-NMR
targets the marginal effect in a stated population and computes it honestly by integrating, whereas plug-in
meta-regression silently reports a conditional-at-the-mean effect and mislabels it as a population effect.
Second, the risk difference and the log risk ratio are *collapsible* in the no-confounding case, so on the
identity and log links this particular gap does not arise. (Aggregation can still bias the log link through
Jensen, as @thm-log-link-mgf shows, but that is variance-driven curvature, not non-collapsibility.) The odds
ratio is the scale on which the two phenomena coincide, which is why binary outcomes are where the fights
happen. Chapter 7 introduced non-collapsibility for a single logistic regression; this section has shown that it
is the same phenomenon as logit aggregation bias, now playing out across a network.

## Notes and references {#sec-agg-notes}

Multilevel network meta-regression was introduced by @phillippo2020mlnmr and developed at length in the
doctoral thesis @phillippo2019thesis, whose Chapter 4 is the source of the aggregation principle treated here.
The individual model @eq-agg-individual-model is their Equation (2) and thesis Equation (4.1b); the aggregate
mean @eq-agg-aggregate-mean is thesis Equation (4.1d); the aggregation theorem @thm-aggregation is the
likelihood identity of thesis Equation (4.1c) and the manuscript's Section 3; and the aggregation-bias
identity @eq-agg-eb is thesis Equation (4.8). The names "individual-level model" and "aggregate-level model"
follow the multilevel-modeling reading in which patients are nested within studies, and the two levels are
linked by integration rather than by the usual random intercept.

The aggregation-bias theorem @thm-aggregation-bias is Jensen's inequality (@thm-jensen) applied to the inverse
link, and it is the same mathematical fact as the ecological bias of aggregate regression (@def-ecological-bias)
diagnosed in Chapter 16 and as the non-collapsibility of marginal effects (@def-non-collapsibility) discussed
in Chapter 7. The leading-order expansion @lem-agg-bias-expansion is the delta-method or Laplace heuristic made
into a theorem with a remainder bound; it is folklore in the ecological-inference literature. The heat-flow
lemma @lem-agg-heat-flow is the observation that Gaussian smoothing is the heat semigroup
$e^{(\tau/2)\partial^2}$; we have not seen it stated for ML-NMR, though it is implicit whenever a closed-form
aggregate mean is derived under normal covariates, and it gives the cleanest account of why the log and probit
links keep closed forms (their inverse links, $\exp$ and $\Phi$, are stable under Gaussian convolution) while
the logit link does not. The probit closed form @prp-agg-probit-closed-form reuses the Gaussian probit integral
of @owen1956, derived in this book as @lem-limits-probit-integral.

The log-link closed form @thm-log-link-mgf is the log-normal mean and is standard; it underlies the
closed-form Poisson aggregate likelihood that Chapter 21 takes up. The logit-normal integral
@eq-agg-logit-integral is the mean of a logit-normal distribution; its non-elementarity (@thm-logit-no-closed-form)
is well known and is the reason ML-NMR for binary outcomes is a numerical-integration method, treated in
Chapter 22 via Sklar's theorem (@sklar1959), Sobol' sequences (@sobol1967), and the quasi-Monte Carlo error
theory descending from the Koksma-Hlawka inequality. The probit substitution
$\mathrm{expit}(z)\approx\Phi(\kappa z)$ mentioned in the remark after @thm-logit-no-closed-form is the
logistic-to-normal slope match; it is an approximation only and is not used in the fitted ML-NMR likelihood,
which integrates numerically.

There is no machine-checked counterpart to this chapter. The Coq development accompanying the book
(@phillippo2019thesis notwithstanding) formalizes the potential-outcomes, propensity-score, MAIC, and STC
material of Parts II to IV but stops short of ML-NMR, whose mathematical content is the numerical analysis of
Chapters 21 and 22 rather than the algebra of the earlier parts; we note this gap in the work log. The
aggregation identity @thm-aggregation is, however, a single application of the chain rule, Fubini's theorem
(@thm-fubini-tonelli), and the tower property (@cor-total-expectation), all of which are formalized in the
probability libraries the development depends on, so a future formalization would be short.

## Exercises {#sec-agg-exercises}

A starred exercise ($\star$) has a full worked solution in Appendix F. The exercises are graded: the first two
are warm-ups and interpretation questions that need only arithmetic and the ideas of the chapter; the later ones
build to the algebra and the proofs. Read the warm-ups even if you skip the proofs, since they carry the applied
message.

::: {#exr-agg-same-mean-different-prediction}
## Warm-up: same mean covariate, different aggregate risk
Two AgD studies enroll patients for the same binary outcome on the logit scale and report the *same* mean
covariate $\bar x$, but study 1's patients are tightly clustered around $\bar x$ while study 2's are widely
spread. Explain in one short paragraph, without any calculation, why the ML-NMR aggregate risk can differ
between the two studies even though their plug-in risks $\mathrm{expit}(\eta(\bar x))$ are identical. Which
study's true risk sits further from its plug-in value, and why? (You are re-deriving in words why matching only
the mean covariate, as first-moment MAIC does, cannot by itself remove aggregation bias.)
:::

::: {#exr-agg-mini-arithmetic}
## Warm-up: the six-point gap by hand
An arm splits evenly into two covariate groups with individual PASI 75 response probabilities $0.60$ and $0.10$.
(a) Compute the true aggregate response as the average of the two risks. (b) Compute the two log-odds, average
them, and apply $\mathrm{expit}$ to obtain the plug-in response. (c) Confirm the plug-in underestimates, and say
which case of @thm-aggregation-bias (convex or concave $g^{-1}$) you are in by checking the sign of the mean
log-odds. (This is the mini-example of @sec-agg-aggregate redone from scratch.)
:::

::: {#exr-agg-prevalence}
## Bias as a function of prevalence ($\star$)
Repeat the logit worked example @exm-agg-logit-discrete with the effect-modifier prevalence changed to
$q=P(x=1)=0.3$, keeping all four parameters $\mu_j=-1,\ \beta_1=0.5,\ \beta_{2,B}=1.0,\ \gamma_B=0.8$.
(a) Recompute the integrated aggregate risks $\theta_{\bullet C},\theta_{\bullet B}$ as the two-point averages
$(1-q)\,\mathrm{expit}(\eta(0))+q\,\mathrm{expit}(\eta(1))$. (b) Recompute the plug-in risks at
$\bar x_j=q=0.3$. (c) Confirm that the plug-in marginal log odds ratio again equals
$\gamma_B+\beta_{2,B}\bar x_j$ exactly, and report the ecological bias of the contrast. (d) Explain, using
@thm-logit-no-closed-form(c), why decreasing $q$ moves both arms' mean linear predictors $m_C,m_B$ downward
and what that does to the sign of each arm's bias.
:::

::: {#exr-agg-identity-uniqueness}
## The identity link is the only universally exact link ($\star$)
Prove that a twice-differentiable link $g$ satisfies $\theta_{\bullet jk}=\theta^{\mathrm{naive}}_{\bullet jk}$
for *every* nondegenerate covariate distribution and every choice of total slope
$\boldsymbol\beta_{\mathrm{tot},k}$ if and only if $g$ is the identity link up to an affine reparameterization,
that is $g^{-1}(z)=a+bz$ with $b\ne0$. (Hint: by @thm-identity-link-exact the condition forces $g^{-1}$ affine
on every interval; deduce $g^{-1}$ is globally affine, and translate this into a statement about $g$.) Conclude
that aggregation bias is unavoidable on any genuinely nonlinear scale, including the logit, log, probit, and
complementary log-log.
:::

::: {#exr-agg-log-multiplicative}
## Variance, not mean, drives the log-link bias
On the log scale with normal covariates, use @thm-log-link-mgf to show that the multiplicative plug-in bias
$\theta_{\bullet jk}/\theta^{\mathrm{naive}}_{\bullet jk}=e^{v/2}$ depends on the covariate distribution only
through the variance $v=\boldsymbol\beta_{\mathrm{tot},k}^\top\boldsymbol\Sigma_j\boldsymbol\beta_{\mathrm{tot},k}$
of the linear predictor and not at all through its mean. Two studies with identical covariate means
$\bar{\mathbf x}_j$ but different covariance matrices therefore have identical plug-in rates but different true
rates; compute the ratio of their true rates when $\boldsymbol\Sigma_j$ is scaled by a factor $c>0$.
:::

::: {#exr-agg-heat-verify}
## Verifying the heat-flow lemma on the three links
Using @lem-agg-heat-flow, verify directly that each of the following is the solution $u(m,\tau)$ of the heat
equation $\partial_\tau u=\tfrac12\partial_m^2 u$ with the stated initial data, and identify which link each
corresponds to. (a) $u(m,\tau)=m$ with $u(m,0)=m$. (b) $u(m,\tau)=e^{m+\tau/2}$ with $u(m,0)=e^m$.
(c) $u(m,\tau)=\Phi(m/\sqrt{1+\tau})$ with $u(m,0)=\Phi(m)$. (d) Explain why no elementary $u$ exists for
$u(m,0)=\mathrm{expit}(m)$, relating your answer to @thm-logit-no-closed-form(d).
:::

::: {#exr-agg-second-moment}
## When first-moment matching is not enough
Two AgD studies report the same covariate mean $\bar x=0$ for a single continuous effect modifier, but study 1
has variance $\sigma_1^2=0.25$ and study 2 has variance $\sigma_2^2=4$. The outcome is binary on the logit
scale with $\eta(x)=\beta_{\mathrm{tot}}\,x$ and $\beta_{\mathrm{tot}}=1$. (a) Using
@thm-logit-no-closed-form(a), show that *both* studies have aggregate risk exactly $\tfrac12$, so that here the
variance does not bias the arm mean. (b) Now shift the baseline to $\eta(x)=0.8+x$ so that the mean linear
predictor is $m=0.8$; using @lem-agg-bias-expansion, estimate the aggregation bias in each study to leading
order and explain why first-moment matching (which equates $\bar x$ but ignores $\sigma^2$) leaves a residual
bias that differs between the two studies. Relate this to the second-moment-matching remark in Chapter 18.
:::

::: {#exr-agg-correlated}
## Closed-form aggregation with two correlated covariates
Let $\mathbf X\sim\mathcal N(\bar{\mathbf x}_j,\boldsymbol\Sigma_j)$ in $\mathbb R^2$ with
$\bar{\mathbf x}_j=(1,2)^\top$ and $\boldsymbol\Sigma_j=\begin{pmatrix}1&0.5\\0.5&2\end{pmatrix}$, log link,
and total slope $\boldsymbol\beta_{\mathrm{tot},k}=(0.4,-0.3)^\top$, with $\mu_j=0$ and $\gamma_k=0.2$.
(a) Compute $m=\mu_j+\gamma_k+\bar{\mathbf x}_j^\top\boldsymbol\beta_{\mathrm{tot},k}$ and
$v=\boldsymbol\beta_{\mathrm{tot},k}^\top\boldsymbol\Sigma_j\boldsymbol\beta_{\mathrm{tot},k}$. (b) Report the
integrated aggregate rate $\theta_{\bullet jk}=e^{m+v/2}$ and the plug-in rate $e^m$. (c) Show that flipping
the sign of the off-diagonal covariance to $-0.5$ changes $v$ and hence the bias, even though the marginal
variances and means are unchanged, and interpret this as the dependence of aggregation bias on the joint, not
merely marginal, covariate distribution.
:::

::: {#exr-agg-nma-reduction}
## Reduction to network meta-analysis
Show that when $\boldsymbol\beta_1=\mathbf 0$ and $\boldsymbol\beta_{2,k}=\mathbf 0$ for every $k$, the linear
predictor @eq-agg-individual-model reduces to $\eta_{jk}=\mu_j+\gamma_k$, the integral
@eq-agg-aggregate-mean reduces to $\theta_{\bullet jk}=g^{-1}(\mu_j+\gamma_k)$ with no dependence on $f_j$, and
hence the aggregate likelihood @eq-agg-aggregate-likelihood is exactly the standard network meta-analysis
likelihood with study baselines $\mu_j$ and treatment effects $\gamma_k$. (This is the NMA special case proved
in full generality in Chapter 23.) Explain why aggregation bias is identically zero in this case for *every*
link, and reconcile this with @thm-aggregation-bias.
:::

::: {#exr-agg-jensen-gap-bound}
## A two-sided bound on the logit aggregation bias
Let $\eta_{jk}(X)\sim\mathcal N(m,\tau)$ on the logit scale. Using $0\le\mathrm{expit}''(z)\le$ its maximum
modulus and the exact second-moment identity $\mathbb E[(\eta-m)^2]=\tau$, prove the nonasymptotic bound
$$
\big|\,\theta_{\bullet jk}-\theta^{\mathrm{naive}}_{\bullet jk}\,\big|\ \le\ \tfrac12\Big(\sup_z|\mathrm{expit}''(z)|\Big)\,\tau
=\tfrac{1}{12\sqrt3}\,\tau,
$$
where $\sup_z|\mathrm{expit}''(z)|=1/(6\sqrt3)$ is attained at $z=\pm\log(2+\sqrt3)$. (Hint: bound the
Taylor remainder of @lem-agg-bias-expansion by the supremum of the second derivative rather than discarding
it, using $\mathrm{expit}(\eta)-\mathrm{expit}(m)-\mathrm{expit}'(m)(\eta-m)=\tfrac12\mathrm{expit}''(\zeta)(\eta-m)^2$.)
Compare this guaranteed bound with the exact bias computed in @exm-agg-logit-discrete.
:::

Solutions to the starred exercises @exr-agg-prevalence and @exr-agg-identity-uniqueness appear in Appendix F.
